source_or_privileged_boundary: A lower-privilege participant who can precreate .kcs in a shared scope, or a repository/archive author who supplies .kcs as a directory or symlink.
closest_control: New stores are chmod 0700, and JSON/schema/hash state is validated.
sink_or_broken_control: The owner-only hardening is skipped for existing stores; open does not use symlink_metadata, check ownership/mode, canonicalize and contain kcs_dir, or compare stored scope_path to root. Snapshot/index then write victim-readable document bytes to that selected store.
impact: An attacker-controlled or attacker-readable store can receive raw/normalized copies of files that only the victim process can read; an aliased legitimate store can also be corrupted across scope boundaries.

steps: Victim opens or re-initializes an existing store.
Schema validation succeeds and permissions remain unchanged.

severity_facts: Raw CAS intentionally stores secrets verbatim.

evidence: crates/kcs-core/src/scope.rs:152-158 explicitly says raw objects contain verbatim secret-bearing bytes and must not be group/world-readable.

crates/kcs-core/src/scope.rs:254-303 and crates/kcs-core/src/cas.rs:60-75,155-176 write new raw bytes using umask-derived file modes.

counterevidence: The demonstrated mode boundary is Unix-specific; non-Unix ACL behavior was not assessed.
A valid writable store and later victim mutation are required.
A 0077 process umask may make newly created raw files owner-only even under a traversable parent, but KCS does not enforce that invariant.
Exposure of bytes already present before open predates the command; the validated impact is the addition of new private bytes after unsafe adoption.

proof_gap: No material Unix proof gap. A second OS account was not created, and non-Unix ACL/ownership behavior remains untested.
remediation_subsumption_decision: Before any read or mutation, reject symlink/non-directory, wrong-owner, or group/world-accessible existing stores, or securely repair an owner-controlled store; this complements rather than subsumes canonical store-root binding and consent-provenance controls.

attack_steps: A lower-trust participant supplies, precreates, or influences a structurally valid existing .kcs store whose Unix ownership or permissions do not provide the expected owner-only boundary.
The victim adopts the scope and Repository::open accepts the store without rejecting or repairing its owner, type, or mode.
The victim later snapshots or indexes a private direct-child file while using an ordinary permissive umask.
KCS writes verbatim raw bytes as a group/world-readable CAS object beneath a traversable store, allowing a different local principal to read data that remained private at the source path.
assumptions: A multi-principal Unix host or shared filesystem enforces ordinary DAC semantics.
The victim adopts a valid existing store that is writable by KCS but readable or traversable by the lower-trust principal.
The victim later adds private content and the process umask does not independently force 0600 objects.
attack_path_facts.context: This is not same-user arbitrary mutation of a private live store. It uses the threat model's in-scope supplied/preseeded-store actor and crosses a distinct Unix principal boundary when KCS adds new private bytes after unsafe adoption.
attack_path_facts.in_scope: yes; pre-existing store adoption, owner-only archive confidentiality, and shared-state contributors are explicit I1/I3 surfaces
attack_path_facts.exposure: not public; local multi-user or shared-filesystem store reached through normal init/open and snapshot/index commands
attack_path_facts.identity: the victim KCS process writes with the victim OS identity; a lower-privileged local principal reads through unsafe store and object modes
attack_path_facts.cross_boundary: yes; victim-only source bytes become readable across an OS-principal filesystem boundary
attack_path_facts.preconditions: plausible but constrained: unsafe supplied or pre-existing store, victim adoption and later mutation, multi-principal access, and a non-0077 umask
attack_path_facts.attacker_control: plausible; the lower-trust archive contributor can control or preserve the supplied store's ownership/mode state without needing victim credentials
attack_path_facts.category: improper ownership and permission validation causing sensitive-data exposure (CWE-276, CWE-732)
mitigations: Fresh stores are explicitly hardened to 0700.
Repository open validates logical store structure.
A 0077 process umask can incidentally produce owner-only raw files.
The demonstrated path is Unix-specific and read-only trusted archives are a legitimate use case.
attack_path_facts.auth_scope: internal-only; lower-privileged local filesystem principal, not administrator or same-user unrestricted private-state access
attack_path_facts.impact_surface: archive confidentiality and integrity on multi-user filesystems
attack_path_facts.target_reach: all new raw objects written into one unsafely adopted store; the retained proof demonstrated one private file
secrets_references: Raw CAS objects contain verbatim document bytes and may include document secrets.
counterevidence: No second OS-account read was executed, though the observed 0600 source, 0755 store, and 0644 raw object establish the Unix DAC result.
A 0077 umask or a securely permissioned trusted store defeats the demonstrated confidentiality path.
Exposure of bytes already present before open is not attributed to KCS; the validated impact is new bytes written after adoption.
blindspots: Non-Unix ACL and ownership behavior was not assessed.
The exact supplied-store transfer mechanism and principal layout remain deployment-specific.
attack_path_facts.confidence: high (0.97) for the Unix mechanism; medium-high for deployment reachability
attack_path_facts.rationale: A supplied-store contributor and a different local OS principal are realistic in-scope actors, so privileged-only suppression does not apply. The disclosure can include private documents, but requires local setup and victim adoption; high impact plus medium likelihood maps to medium.
